questions.question: What two things must be true for two lines to be skew?
options: They do not intersect and are not parallel.
They lie in $\mathbb R^2$ and have different slopes.

questions.question: In what ambient dimension can skew lines first occur?
Why can two lines in $\mathbb R^2$ not be skew?
options: Plane lines have no direction vectors.
Every pair of plane lines is parallel.
Nonparallel lines in the plane intersect.

questions.question: Which relationship is ruled out by saying that two lines are skew?
What geometric lesson do skew lines illustrate?
options: Higher-dimensional spaces have line relationships not possible in the plane.
Every line relation in space already occurs in the plane, regardless of the specific input chosen.
Parallelism has no meaning in $\mathbb R^3$.

questions.question: Are the $x$-axis and the line through $(0,1,1)$ in direction $(0,1,0)$ skew in $\mathbb R^3$?
options: No, because skew lines cannot occur in $\mathbb R^3$.

questions.question: Can two distinct lines in $\mathbb R^2$ be skew?
options: Yes, if they do not pass through the origin.

questions.question: The lines $\ell_1(t)=(t,0,0)$ and $\ell_2(s)=(0,s,1)$ have directions $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$. Are the directions parallel?
Do $\ell_1(t)=(t,0,0)$ and $\ell_2(s)=(0,s,1)$ intersect?
What is the relation between $\ell_1(t)=(t,0,0)$ and $\ell_2(s)=(0,s,1)$?
Why is checking only the direction vectors insufficient to prove two lines are skew?
options: Direction vectors determine the base points.
Intersection does not matter for skewness.

questions.question: How do skew lines differ from distinct parallel lines?
options: Distinct parallel lines are always skew.
Parallel lines require dimension at least three, no matter which values are selected.
Skew lines are not parallel; distinct parallel lines have the same direction.

questions.question: How do skew lines differ from crossing lines in $\mathbb R^3$?
options: Crossing lines intersect; skew lines do not.
Skew lines intersect at exactly one point.
There is no difference in $\mathbb R^3$.

questions.question: Are $\ell_1(t)=(t,t,0)$ and $\ell_2(s)=(1+s,1+s,2)$ skew?
options: No; they are parallel and distinct.

questions.question: Are $\ell_1(t)=(t,0,0)$ and $\ell_2(s)=(0,s,0)$ skew?
options: Yes; all nonparallel lines in $\mathbb R^3$ are skew.
Yes; their directions are not parallel.
No; they intersect at the origin.

questions.question: Which pair of lines is a plausible skew pair in $\mathbb R^3$?
Why is the statement “nonparallel lines do not intersect” false in $\mathbb R^3$?
options: Nonparallel lines are always parallel after reparametrisation.
Nonparallel lines may either intersect or be skew.
All nonparallel lines must be skew.
Nonparallel lines in $\mathbb R^3$ always intersect.

questions.question: What must be solved, besides a scalar-multiple test, to decide whether two space lines are skew?
options: The system equating their parametric coordinates.
Only the determinant of one direction vector.
Only the length of each direction vector.
Only whether the starting points are different.

questions.question: Let $\ell_1(t)=(t,0,0)$ and $\ell_2(s)=(1,s,1+s)$. Are they skew?
options: No; both lie in the plane $z=0$.

questions.question: For $\ell_1(t)=(t,0,0)$ and $\ell_2(s)=(1,s,a)$, which value of $a$ makes the lines intersect?
